question: What if Clive had lost at Plassey in 1757?
short: Plassey was won by a bribe more than a battle: the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar held his troops back. Lose it, and the East India Company stays a trading company with forts on the Bengal coast for a while longer. But the Mughal empire had already broken into rival states, Britain and France were fighting over them, and Lancashire's machines were coming. British rule is the likeliest outcome either way, just later and maybe smaller; India's fall from about a quarter of world output started before Plassey.

divergence.text: Mir Jafar's cavalry fight for Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey instead of standing aside.

plausibility_note: Medium: the battle really did hinge on one man's choice, but the forces that made a Company conquest possible were bigger than one day.

steps.title: A quarter of the world's output
steps.text: Angus Maddison estimated that India produced about a quarter of world output around 1700, roughly as much as all of Western Europe. Bengal's cotton and silk cloth were sold from Japan to London. These are rough estimates built on population more than on prices.

sources.cite: Angus Maddison, The World Economy: A Millennial Perspective (2001)

steps.title: An empire breaking into kingdoms
steps.text: After Aurangzeb died in 1707 the Mughal governors of Bengal, Hyderabad and Awadh ruled as kings in all but name, while the Marathas spread from the Deccan. In 1739 Nader Shah of Iran sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne. Plassey happened in a country already split into rival states.

sources.cite: C. A. Bayly, Indian Society and the Making of the British Empire (1988)

steps.title: Plassey: the battle that was bought
steps.text: Robert Clive had about 3,000 men against an army of perhaps 50,000. Mir Jafar, promised the throne, kept his large force out of the fight; rain soaked the Nawab's powder. Siraj ud-Daulah fled and was killed, and Mir Jafar became a Company puppet.

steps.title: The right to tax Bengal
steps.text: After beating the Mughal emperor and the Nawab of Awadh at Buxar in 1764, the Company got the diwani in 1765: the right to collect Bengal's land revenue. Its trade was now paid for by Bengal's own taxes. Five years later a famine killed perhaps a third of Bengal's people.

steps.title: Bengal stays with the Nawabs
steps.text: Siraj ud-Daulah, who had already taken Calcutta once in 1756, could push the Company back to trading posts on his terms. The British would still hold Madras and Bombay and would still be fighting France. So the branch most likely delays Company rule in Bengal by years or decades rather than preventing it.

steps.title: The machines come anyway
steps.text: Broadberry, Custodis and Gupta find India's income per head already sliding against Britain's before 1757, and cheap machine-made cotton from Lancashire undercut hand weavers everywhere after 1800. An independent Bengal still faces that. Prasannan Parthasarathi argues the gap came from what British states did (protect cotton, push coal), which a Bengal state could in principle have copied. That is where this branch is truly open.

sources.cite: Stephen Broadberry, Johann Custodis and Bishnupriya Gupta, India and the great divergence, Explorations in Economic History 55 (2015)
Prasannan Parthasarathi, Why Europe Grew Rich and Asia Did Not (2011)

steps.title: A Maratha subcontinent?
steps.text: The Marathas were the strongest Indian power of the 1750s, until the Afghan Ahmad Shah Durrani shattered their army at Panipat in 1761. Without a Company Bengal paying for sepoy armies, a recovered Maratha confederacy is the most obvious rival to dominate the north. Wild, but it uses the real contenders.

views.name: William Dalrymple
views.claim: A company backed by Indian bankers and a divided elite took India in a few contingent decades.
views.for: Plassey and Buxar turned on bribes and defections.
views.against: Contingency at one battle does not make the whole outcome contingent.

views.name: C. A. Bayly
views.claim: Indian merchants and elites helped build Company rule; it grew out of the Mughal successor states.
views.for: Revenue systems and banking networks carried straight over.
views.against: Plays down the violence and the drain of revenue to Britain.

views.name: Broadberry, Custodis and Gupta
views.claim: India's relative decline began before colonial rule.
views.for: Wage and output series from the 1600s.
views.against: Early Indian data are thin, and other scholars read them differently.

unknowns: How large India's economy really was around 1700.
Whether the Company's directors in London would have backed a second try after a defeat.
How much of Bengal's later decline was Company policy and how much world markets.
